rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all eight peaks and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Halve the gradient slope to test separation of the crowded middle cluster and final pair. The initial run's short elution window leaves room to improve resolution while keeping the last peak near or below 10 minutes.

Raise temperature while holding the gradient fixed to probe selectivity for the sole unresolved pair. This may also shorten retention, creating room for further resolution improvements without a time penalty.
Test lower temperature to move away from the co-elutions seen at 40–50 C. Shortening the gradient slightly should offset increased retention and help keep the last peak within 10 minutes.

Test whether higher temperature carries the overlapping middle peaks through a selectivity crossover and separates them again. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates this effect, with the last peak expected to remain below 10 minutes.

At 60 C only one pair remains unresolved, so test a steeper gradient to shift its relative retention away from the apparent crossover. This also shortens the elution window, though the other close pairs will need monitoring.

This gives a slightly shallower slope than injection 6, targeting R ≥ 1.5 for both early close pairs without sacrificing the later pair's narrow resolution margin. The final organic fraction remains above the estimated composition at which the last peak eluted.

Injection 7 already achieves the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Shift the gradient window upward while preserving its slope to test whether all peaks can elute sooner without losing full resolution.

Slightly flatten the shifted gradient to recover separation of the early close pairs while retaining some of injection 8's time savings. Injection 7 remains the maximum-score fallback; monitor the later cluster for a new selectivity crossover.

Test a lower starting organic fraction to strengthen early-pair separation, combined with a steeper gradient to shorten late retention. This explores a different route to a faster fully resolved method while retaining injection 7 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Explore lower-temperature selectivity with a shorter gradient, seeking a different fully resolved elution pattern. Injection 7 already attains the maximum CRF; this run tests whether a faster alternative exists outside the narrow high-temperature optimum.

Slightly flatten the low-temperature gradient to improve its sole unresolved pair and test for a second fully resolved method near the 10-minute limit. Injection 7 remains the faster, maximum-score benchmark.

Test intermediate-temperature selectivity with a faster gradient, seeking a fully resolved alternative to injection 7. The temperature-dependent order changes suggest another useful separation window may exist between the conditions already sampled.

Lower temperature one step from injection 13 to widen its unresolved middle pair while checking that the neighboring pair stays separated. This tests the intermediate-temperature separation window at a fixed gradient; injection 7 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Return to the successful high-temperature region and flatten injection 10's gradient to recover its close-pair separations. The lower starting fraction may provide a fully resolved alternative with better resolution margins than injection 7 while remaining below 10 minutes.

Increase the slope only slightly from injection 7, probing the fastest fully resolved boundary between injections 6 and 7. This should shorten retention modestly, although the early critical pair may fall just below R = 1.5.

The high-temperature speed boundary is now bracketed: injection 7 is fully resolved, while injection 16 is slightly too steep. Test a warmer, higher-starting-organic variant of the promising 25 C method to seek a second full-resolution region with shorter retention.

Lower temperature to improve selectivity in the early cluster, while raising the starting organic fraction to offset the retention increase. The slightly shallower slope may also improve the remaining close pair; injection 7 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Flatten injection 18's gradient to improve its sole unresolved pair, using the available retention-time margin below 10 minutes. This tests for a fully resolved low-temperature alternative while preserving injection 7 as the best method.

Raise the starting organic fraction to shorten the fully resolved low-temperature method, while flattening the gradient to compensate for reduced separation of its critical pair. Injection 7 remains the fastest maximum-score method found.

Flatten injection 20's gradient to recover its sole unresolved pair, with enough time margin to remain below 10 minutes. This seeks another maximum-score method; injection 7 remains the fastest fully resolved option.

Raise temperature one step from injection 20 to test whether selectivity can resolve its sole deficient pair without the longer gradient required at 25 C. This also targets shorter retention, while injection 7 remains the fastest maximum-score method.

Flatten injection 22's gradient to target its sole unresolved pair, checking that the neighboring pair retains sufficient separation. This may provide full resolution near 8 minutes at moderate temperature; injection 7 remains the fastest maximum-score benchmark.

Raise temperature one step from the fully resolved injection 19 to shorten retention. The lower starting fraction may avoid the final-pair overlap seen in injection 23, while injection 7 remains the fastest maximum-score method.

Use the final injection to test a slightly shallower gradient near the fastest maximum-score method, improving the early critical pairs while checking the later pair's resolution margin.
